scenes.narration: The last chapter of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was written long after the fame. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman (17 March 1920 – 15 August 1975) was a Bangladeshi politician, revolutionary, statesman, activist, and diarist who was the founding president of Bangladesh. As the leader of Bangladesh, he led the country as its president and prime minister from 1972 until his assassination in a coup d'état in 1975.

The whole life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman reads like a single decision repeated. Born in an aristocratic Bengali Muslim family in Tungipara, Mujib emerged as a student activist in the province of Bengal during the final years of the British Raj. He was a member of the All-India Muslim League, supported Muslim nationalism, and advocated for the establishment of Pakistan in his early political career.

Between the birth and the legend of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman lie the years that actually decide it. In 1949, he became part of a liberal, secular and left-wing faction which later became the Awami League. In the 1950s, he was elected to Pakistan's parliament where he defended the rights of East Bengal.

The reputation of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was built in the middle, not at the edges. Mujib served 13 years in prison during the British Raj and Pakistani rule. By the 1960s, Mujib adopted Bengali nationalism and soon became the undisputed leader of East Pakistan.

Somebody like Sheikh Mujibur Rahman should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. He became popular for opposing West Pakistan's political, ethnic and institutional discrimination against the Bengalis of East Pakistan; leading the six-point autonomy movement, he challenged the rule of Pakistani president Ayub Khan. In 1970, Mujib led the Awami League to win Pakistan's first general election.

The life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman begins far from where the story usually starts. When the Pakistani military junta under President Yahya Khan refused to transfer power, he gave the 7 March speech in 1971 where he vaguely called out for the independence movement. In the late hours of 25 March 1971, the Pakistan Army arrested Sheikh Mujib on charges of treason and carried out a genocide against the Bengali civilians of East Pakistan.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Bengali nationalists declared him the head of the Provisional Government of Bangladesh, while he was confined in a jail in West Pakistan. After the independence of Bangladesh, Mujib returned to Bangladesh in January 1972 as the leader of a war-devastated country.

To understand where Sheikh Mujibur Rahman ended up, start with where Sheikh Mujibur Rahman began. His foreign policy during the time was dominated by the principle "friendship to all and malice to none". He remained a close ally to Gandhi's India and Brezhnev's Soviet Union, while balancing ties with the United States.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman ran through years nobody filmed. Mujib's government proved largely unsuccessful in curbing political and economic anarchy and corruption in post-independence Bangladesh, which ultimately gave rise to a left-wing insurgency. To quell the insurgency, he formed Jatiya Rakkhi Bahini, a special paramilitary force similar to the Gestapo, which was involved in various human rights abuses, massacres, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and rapes.

Each stage of the life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman made the next stage possible. Mujib's four-year regime was the only socialist period in Bangladesh's history, which was marked with huge economic mismanagement and failure, leading to the high mortality rate in the deadly famine of 1974. On 15 August 1975, he was assassinated along with most of his family members in his Dhanmondi 32 residence in a coup d'état.

The people who knew Sheikh Mujibur Rahman young describe someone already restless. Sheikh Mujib's post-independence legacy remains divisive among Bangladeshis due to his economic mismanagement, the famine of 1974, human rights violations, and authoritarianism. Nevertheless, most Bangladeshis credit him for leading the country to independence in 1971 and restoring the Bengali sovereignty after over two centuries following the Battle of Plassey in 1757, for which he is honoured as Bangabandhu (lit. 'Friend of Bengal').

What Sheikh Mujibur Rahman built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. His 7 March speech in 1971 is recognized by UNESCO for its historic value, and was listed in the Memory of the World Register. Many of his diaries and travelogues were published many years after his death and have been translated into several languages.

By the time Sheikh Mujibur Rahman reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Mujib was born on 17 March 1920 into the Bengali Muslim aristocratic Sheikh family of the village of Tungipara in Gopalganj sub-division of Faridpur district in the province of Bengal in British India. His father Sheikh Lutfur Rahman was a sheristadar (law clerk) in the courthouse of Gopalganj; Mujib's mother Sheikh Sayera Khatun was a housewife.

The rise of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Mujib's father Sheikh Lutfur Rahman was a Taluqdar in Tungipara, owning landed property, around 100 Bighas of cultivable land. His clan's ancestors were Zamindars of Faridpur Mahakumar, however due to successive turns in the family fortune over generations had turned them middle class.

Setbacks came early for Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and the response to them is the real story. The Sheikh clan of Tungipara are descended from the Sufi Dervish, Sheikh Abdul Awal Dervish, who had come to preach Islam who had come with a group of Muslim missionaries likely from Eastern Iran, Mujib was an eighth generation descendant of him. Mujib was the eldest son and third child in the family of four daughters (Fatima, Achia, Helen, Laili) and two sons (Mujib, Naser).

The legacy of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman outlived the circumstances that produced it. As a child, Mujib was described as "compassionate and very energetic", either playing or roaming around, feeding birds, monkeys and dogs. I was not a very good player but still had a good position in the school team...

Few lives travel as far as that of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and the distance is the point. He returned to formal education after four years owing to the severity of the surgery and slow recovery. Mujib was 18 years old when he was married to eight years old Fazilatunnesa, widely known in Bangladesh as Bangamata (lit. 'Mother of Bengal') or Begum Mujib, in an arranged marriage, according to the custom of the region at that time.

The childhood of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman contains the adult in small print. At the Gopalganj Missionary School, Mujib's political passion was noticed by Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, who was visiting the area along with A. At the time, Calcutta was the capital of British Bengal and the largest city in undivided India.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman — in that order. He studied liberal arts, including political science, at the Islamia College of Calcutta and lived in Baker Hostel. Islamia College was one of the leading educational institutions for the Muslims of Bengal.

The turning point in the life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman looked like a failure at the time. During his time in Calcutta, Sheikh Mujib became involved in the politics of the Bengal Provincial Muslim League, the All India Muslim Students Federation, the Indian independence movement and the Pakistan movement. In 1943, he was elected as a councillor of the Muslim League.

Every biography of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In 1944, he was elected as secretary of the Faridpur District Association, a Calcutta-based association of residents from Faridpur. In 1946, at the height of the Pakistan movement, Mujib was elected as General Secretary of the Islamia College Students Union in Calcutta.

The education of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman happened mostly outside any school. Suhrawardy was responsible for creating 36 trade unions in Bengal, including unions for sailors, railway workers, jute and cotton mills workers, rickshaw pullers, cart drivers and other working class groups. Mujib assisted Suhrawardy in these efforts and also worked to ensure protection for Muslim families during the violent days in the run up to partition.

What Sheikh Mujibur Rahman wanted at the start and what Sheikh Mujibur Rahman got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. In 1947, Sheikh Mujib also joined the "United Bengal Movement" which was organized under the leadership of Suhrawardy, Abul Hashim, Sarat Chandra Bose and others to form an undivided independent Bengal outside the jurisdiction of India and Pakistan. Later, when the creation of the states of India and Pakistan was confirmed, a referendum was held to decide the fate of the Bengali Muslim-dominated Sylhet District of Assam Province.

The defining trait of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Sheikh Mujib worked as an organizer and campaigner for inclusion in Pakistan in the Sylhet referendum. In his autobiography, he expressed his displeasure about the non-adherence of Karimganj to Pakistan despite winning the referendum and the various geographical inadequacies of East Pakistan during the demarcation of the partition.

Those who met Sheikh Mujibur Rahman at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. After the partition of India, Mujib was admitted into the Law Department of the University of Dhaka. The university was created in 1921 as a residential university modelled on Oxford and Cambridge where students would be affiliated with colleges; but its residential character was dramatically changed after partition and students became affiliated with departments.

The private years of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman explain the public decades better than any speech. Mujib suffered repeated bouts of police detention due to his ability to instigate opposition protests against the Pakistani government. In 1949, Mujib was expelled from Dhaka University on charges of inciting employees against the university.

The family Sheikh Mujibur Rahman came from matters more than the legends admit. After 61 years, in 2010, the university withdrew its famously politically motivated expulsion order. Mujib emerged as a major opposition figure in Pakistani politics between 1948 and 1971.

The first real success of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. He had an uncanny ability to remember people by their first name regardless of whether they were political leaders, workers, or ordinary citizens. Mujib founded the East Pakistan Students' League on 4 January 1948 as the student wing of the Muslim League in East Bengal.

The last chapter of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was written long after the fame. During the visit of Governor General Muhammad Ali Jinnah to Dhaka, it was declared that Urdu will be the sole national language of Pakistan. Mujib became embroiled in the language movement, as well as left-wing trade unionism among Bengali factions of the Muslim League.

The whole life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman reads like a single decision repeated. Bengali factions eventually split away and formed the Awami Muslim League in 1949. East Pakistan's Intelligence Branch compiled many secret reports on his movements and political activities.

Between the birth and the legend of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman lie the years that actually decide it. The All Pakistan Awami Muslim League was founded on 23 June 1949 at the Rose Garden mansion on K. Das Lane in Old Dhaka, which was organized by Yar Mohammad Khan and Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani.

The reputation of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was built in the middle, not at the edges. Seeking to represent and secure votes from both Muslims and religious minorities, including Bengali Hindus and Pakistani Christians, "Muslim" was eventually removed from the League's name. Suhrawardy joined the party within a few years and became its main leader.

Somebody like Sheikh Mujibur Rahman should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Prior to partition, Suhrawardy mooted the idea of an independent United Bengal. In Pakistan, Suhrawardy reportedly preferred to preserve the unity of Pakistan in a federal framework, while Mujib supported autonomy and was open to the idea of East Bengali independence.

The life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman begins far from where the story usually starts. At the provincial level, the League was led by Sheikh Mujib who was given a free rein over the party's activities by Suhrawardy. The Awami League veered away from the left-wing extremism of its founding president Maulana Bhashani.
